rubric.why: Identifies the atom and the electron removal that defines the first ionization energy.
rubric.description: State that one electron is removed from an isolated gaseous atom to form a positive ion.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark when the answer identifies a gaseous (or isolated) atom, removal of one electron, and formation of a positive ion.

rubric.why: Defines ionization energy as an energy requirement and specifies that this is the first removal.
rubric.description: Define it as the energy required for the first electron removal.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing the process as requiring energy and identifying it as the first electron removed.

modelAnswer: First ionization energy is the energy required to remove one electron from the outermost shell of an isolated gaseous atom.
The atom forms a unipositive ion: X(g) → X⁺(g) + e⁻.

items.followUp: Write four common types of chemical bond.

rubric.why: Recognizes two of the common types of chemical bond.
rubric.description: Name ionic and covalent bonds.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for both ionic (or electrovalent) and covalent.

rubric.why: Completes the required list of four bond types.
rubric.description: Name coordinate covalent and metallic bonds.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for both coordinate (or dative) covalent and metallic.

modelAnswer: Four types of chemical bond are ionic (electrovalent), covalent, coordinate covalent (dative), and metallic bonds.

items.followUp: What is percentage mass/volume concentration? Give an example.

rubric.why: Shows that percentage mass/mass is based on solute mass compared with total solution mass.
rubric.description: Define percentage mass/mass using the mass ratio multiplied by 100.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct mass-of-solute to mass-of-solution ratio and multiplication by 100.

rubric.why: Provides a numerical example consistent with the definition.
rubric.description: Give a correct example with the percentage calculated.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a valid example; for instance, 10 g of solute in 100 g of solution gives 10% m/m.

modelAnswer: Percentage mass/mass is the mass of solute present in 100 parts by mass of solution.
% m/m = (mass of solute ÷ mass of solution) × 100.
Example: 10 g of salt in 100 g of solution gives (10 g ÷ 100 g) × 100 = 10% m/m.

rubric.why: States the defining tendency of an electropositive element.
rubric.description: State that electropositivity is a tendency to lose electrons.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying electron loss as the defining property.

rubric.why: Identifies the result of losing electrons.
rubric.description: State that electron loss forms positive ions.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that the element forms positive ions or cations.

modelAnswer: Electropositivity is the tendency of an atom to lose electrons and form positive ions (cations).

items.followUp: Write the equation for the reaction of chlorine with cold, dilute sodium hydroxide.

rubric.why: Checks the correct products for chlorine reacting with hot, concentrated sodium hydroxide.
rubric.description: Write the correct products: sodium chloride, sodium chlorate, and water.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for all three correct products.

rubric.why: Checks the correctly balanced equation and conditions.
rubric.description: Write and balance the reaction equation.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the balanced equation 3Cl₂ + 6NaOH → 5NaCl + NaClO₃ + 3H₂O, with hot concentrated conditions identified.

modelAnswer: With hot, concentrated sodium hydroxide, chlorine undergoes disproportionation.
3Cl₂ + 6NaOH → 5NaCl + NaClO₃ + 3H₂O

items.followUp: Write any three differences between Rutherford’s atomic model and Bohr’s atomic model.

rubric.why: Contrasts Rutherford’s unrestricted electron paths with Bohr’s permitted orbits.
rubric.description: Compare the orbits of electrons in the two models.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that Rutherford allowed any orbit while Bohr proposed definite or fixed orbits.

rubric.why: Shows that Bohr assigned definite energies to the permitted orbits.
rubric.description: Compare the energy of electrons in the two models.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for contrasting the absence of definite energy levels in Rutherford’s model with Bohr’s fixed energy levels.

rubric.why: Contrasts the stability problem in Rutherford’s model with Bohr’s stable stationary orbits.
rubric.description: Compare the stability of the atom in the two models.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that Rutherford’s model could not explain atomic stability while Bohr’s stable orbits did.

rubric.why: Tests the models’ ability to explain atomic line spectra.
rubric.description: Compare their explanation of the line spectrum.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that Rutherford could not explain the line spectrum and Bohr explained the hydrogen spectrum.

rubric.why: Contrasts predicted radiation from orbiting electrons with Bohr’s non-radiating stationary orbits.
rubric.description: Compare energy radiation by orbiting electrons.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that Rutherford’s orbiting electrons would radiate energy, whereas electrons in Bohr’s stationary orbits do not.

modelAnswer: Rutherford’s model allowed electrons to revolve around the nucleus in any orbit; Bohr proposed only certain permitted orbits.
Rutherford’s model had no definite electron energy levels; Bohr assigned a definite energy to each permitted orbit.
Rutherford’s model could not explain atomic stability; Bohr’s stationary orbits made the atom stable.
Rutherford’s model could not explain the hydrogen line spectrum; Bohr’s model explained it using electron transitions between energy levels.
In Rutherford’s model, revolving electrons should radiate energy and lose it; in Bohr’s stationary orbits, electrons do not radiate energy.

items.followUp: Classify solutions as mixtures and give one example of each type of mixture.

rubric.why: Defines a mixture as a physical combination rather than a chemical compound.
rubric.description: Define a mixture.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that a mixture is a physical combination of two or more substances.

rubric.why: Identifies a homogeneous mixture and gives a suitable example.
rubric.description: Describe a homogeneous mixture and give an example.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying its uniform composition and giving a valid example such as salt solution or air.

rubric.why: Identifies a heterogeneous mixture and gives a suitable example.
rubric.description: Describe a heterogeneous mixture and give an example.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying its non-uniform composition and giving a valid example such as sand and water.

rubric.why: Adds characteristic properties of mixtures that distinguish them from compounds.
rubric.description: State that components can be present in variable proportions and separated physically.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for either variable proportions or separation by physical methods.

modelAnswer: A mixture is a physical combination of two or more substances that are not chemically combined.
Its components can be present in variable proportions and can be separated by physical methods.
Homogeneous mixture: it has a uniform composition throughout; for example, salt solution.
Heterogeneous mixture: it has a non-uniform composition; for example, sand and water.

items.followUp: Explain the formation of an ionic bond in magnesium oxide (MgO).

rubric.why: Identifies the valence-electron arrangements that allow sodium to transfer one electron to chlorine.
rubric.description: Give the electronic configurations of sodium and chlorine.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for Na = 2,8,1 and Cl = 2,8,7.

rubric.why: Describes the electron transfer that forms the ions.
rubric.description: Explain the transfer of one electron from sodium to chlorine.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that sodium loses one electron and chlorine gains it.

rubric.why: Checks that the correct oppositely charged ions are formed.
rubric.description: Identify the ions formed.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for Na⁺ and Cl⁻.

rubric.why: States the force that holds the ions together and defines the ionic bond.
rubric.description: Explain the attraction forming the ionic bond.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions.

rubric.why: Connects the ion formation to the formula and example compound.
rubric.description: Name the compound formed and give its formula.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying sodium chloride as NaCl.

modelAnswer: Sodium has the electronic configuration 2,8,1, while chlorine has 2,8,7.
A sodium atom transfers its outermost electron to a chlorine atom.
Sodium forms Na⁺ (2,8) and chlorine forms Cl⁻ (2,8,8), giving both ions stable outer shells.
The electrostatic attraction between these oppositely charged ions is an ionic bond.
The ions combine in a 1:1 ratio to form sodium chloride, NaCl.
